title: Argentina Was Richer Than France. What Happened?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1913, if you were a young European looking for a better life, there was one country that kept coming up.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Not America. Not Canada. Argentina.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It had some of the richest farmland on Earth.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Its capital was building wide boulevards, grand opera houses and the first subway in Latin America.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And on average, Argentines earned more than the French and more than the Germans.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Even in 1947, after two world wars, Argentina was still one of the ten richest countries on the planet.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Now look at it today. Argentina has defaulted on its debts nine times.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1989, prices in its shops rose by around five thousand percent in a single year.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And many Argentines still keep their savings in US dollars, hidden at home, because they do not trust their own money.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So how does a country go from richer than France to broke, again and again?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It wasn't a war. It wasn't a famine. It wasn't a single bad leader.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: To find out, we have to go back to the moment Argentina found its fortune.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And it all started with grass.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: This is the Pampas. A sea of flat, fertile grassland bigger than most countries in Europe.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: No mountains to cross, no thick forest to clear. Just endless grass, rain and rich black soil.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For most of history, that grass fed wild cattle and not much else.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina had the land, but it had a problem.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The people who wanted to buy its beef and grain lived on the other side of an ocean.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And meat goes bad long before a sailing ship can cross the Atlantic.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Then, in the 1870s, everything changed at once.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: First came the railways.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: British investors poured money into Argentina, and British companies laid thousands of kilometres of track.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Every line ran the same way: from the farms in the interior straight to the port of Buenos Aires.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Second came the cold. French engineers had worked out how to freeze meat on board a ship.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Suddenly, a steak from the Pampas could reach a dinner table in London or Paris, still fresh.

segments.speaker: BRITISH_INVESTOR
segments.text: So, we build the railway. You send the beef. We buy the beef.

segments.speaker: RANCH_OWNER
segments.text: And who owns the railway?

segments.speaker: BRITISH_INVESTOR
segments.text: We do.

segments.speaker: RANCH_OWNER
segments.text: And the ships?

segments.speaker: BRITISH_INVESTOR
segments.text: Also us.

segments.speaker: RANCH_OWNER
segments.text: And the banks that lend me the money?

segments.speaker: BRITISH_INVESTOR
segments.text: Do you want to get rich or not?

segments.speaker: RANCH_OWNER
segments.text: Pass me the pen.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It was a fantastic deal for both sides, at least at first.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina became one of the biggest exporters of beef, wheat, corn and wool in the world.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Money flowed in faster than the country could spend it.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And people followed the money. Between 1870 and 1914, nearly six million Europeans sailed to Argentina, mostly from Italy and Spain.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: More than three million of them stayed.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the 1890s, in parts of Buenos Aires, you were more likely to hear Italian than the local Spanish.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Buenos Aires earned a nickname: the Paris of South America.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Its rich families shipped their furniture from France, sent their sons to European universities and built mansions that would not look out of place on the Champs-Élysées.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: There was a saying in Europe at the time. If someone was extremely wealthy, people said they were as rich as an Argentine.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By 1913, the country was a success story that the whole world was watching. But look closely at that map again.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Every railway line led to one port. Almost every ship sailed to the same few buyers.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And almost all the best land belonged to a small group of very rich families.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina had built a machine that turned grass into gold. It just hadn't built much of anything else.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: As long as the world kept buying, that didn't matter. Then, one day, the world stopped buying.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In October 1929, the New York stock market crashed, and the Great Depression spread around the world.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Factories closed. Families stopped buying.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And the price of beef and wheat, the two things Argentina sold, collapsed.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For a country that earned almost everything from exports, this was a disaster.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Britain, its biggest customer, began favouring food from its own empire.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The ships that used to leave Buenos Aires full now left half empty.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And then something happened that would shape the next fifty years.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina had become a democracy in 1912, when it gave men the secret ballot.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But in September 1930, with the economy falling apart, the army marched into Buenos Aires and removed the elected president.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It was the country's first military coup of the twentieth century. It would not be the last.

segments.speaker: GENERAL
segments.text: Don't worry. We're only here until things calm down.

segments.speaker: CLERK
segments.text: How long is that?

segments.speaker: GENERAL
segments.text: A few months. A year at most.

segments.speaker: CLERK
segments.text: Temporary. Got it.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Over the next half century, the army took power again and again.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Elected governments came and went. And every new government tore up the plans of the one before it.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That pattern, more than any single policy, is the thread that runs through this whole story. Remember it.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But first, Argentina tried to fix its biggest weakness.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: If selling food to the world was too risky, maybe the answer was to stop depending on the world altogether.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Quick pause. If you're enjoying the story so far, subscribe to the channel. It's free, and unlike the peso, it holds its value.
segments.ctaText: It's free. And unlike the peso, it holds its value.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1946, Argentina elected a former army colonel named Juan Domingo Perón.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And no single person has shaped the country's economy more, for better or for worse, depending on who you ask.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Perón's big idea was simple. Argentina should stop being a farm for Europe and start making things for itself.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Instead of selling beef and buying cars, radios and machines from abroad, it would build its own factories and make them at home.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: To protect those new factories, the government made imported goods expensive with high taxes and strict limits.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It bought the British-owned railways and put them in state hands.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It took control of the grain trade, buying crops from farmers at low prices and selling them abroad at higher ones,

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: using the difference to pay for industry and social programmes.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For working people, especially in the cities, life got noticeably better.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Wages rose. Workers got paid holidays, pensions and new rights.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Millions of Argentines felt, for the first time, that the country's wealth belonged to them too.

segments.speaker: WORKER
segments.text: Boss, our new radios are ready! Made right here in Argentina!

segments.speaker: FACTORY_OWNER
segments.text: Wonderful. How do they compare to the foreign ones?

segments.speaker: WORKER
segments.text: Twice the price. But I helped build it, and next month I get my first paid holiday.

segments.speaker: FACTORY_OWNER
segments.text: And who will buy them?

segments.speaker: WORKER
segments.text: Everyone. The foreign ones cost three times as much now.

segments.speaker: FACTORY_OWNER
segments.text: Then let's build another factory.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: This is where historians and economists still argue, and both sides have a real case.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Supporters say Perón gave ordinary workers dignity and a share of the national wealth that the old ranching elite never would have.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: They point out that the factories, unions and welfare system he built became the backbone of Argentina's middle class.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Critics say the plan had a hidden cost. Protected factories never had to compete, so many stayed inefficient.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Paying farmers less discouraged them from growing more, just when the country needed exports to pay for factory machines.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And when the money ran short, the government did something that would become a very bad habit.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It printed more of it.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1955, Perón himself was overthrown by another military coup. He went into exile for almost eighteen years.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But his movement never went away.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For decades, Argentine politics would swing back and forth between his followers and his opponents,

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: each side undoing what the other had built.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And underneath all of that swinging, one problem kept growing quietly in the background.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That problem was inflation, prices rising year after year.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And to understand why it never went away, you need to understand a trap.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Imagine a government that promises more than it can afford: more jobs, more pensions, more support for factories.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Taxes don't cover it. Borrowing is hard because lenders don't trust you.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So the central bank simply creates more money to pay the bills.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For a while, it feels great. Everyone has more pesos.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But there are no more goods in the shops than before. So shopkeepers raise prices.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Workers demand higher wages to keep up. The government prints even more to pay them. And round and round it goes.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Through the 1950s, 60s and 70s, Argentina was stuck in this loop.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Civilian governments and military ones took turns, and almost all of them leaned on the printing press.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1976 the army seized power once more and ran a brutal dictatorship until 1983.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It borrowed heavily from foreign banks, and Argentina's debt ballooned.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: When the generals finally gave up power after losing the Falklands War against Britain in 1982,

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: they left behind a mountain of debt and an economy close to breaking.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The new democratic governments inherited that mess. They tried new currencies, price freezes and emergency plans. None of them stuck.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And in 1989, the loop finally spun out of control.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In July 1989 alone, prices rose by about two hundred percent. In one month.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Over the whole year, they rose by around five thousand percent.

segments.speaker: SHOPPER
segments.text: Good morning! How much for the bread?

segments.speaker: SHOPKEEPER
segments.text: Ten thousand australes.

segments.speaker: SHOPPER
segments.text: Perfect, I'll come back after work.

segments.speaker: SHOPPER
segments.text: I'm back! Ten thousand, right?

segments.speaker: SHOPKEEPER
segments.text: Twelve thousand.

segments.speaker: SHOPPER
segments.text: It's the same bread!

segments.speaker: SHOPKEEPER
segments.text: Same bread. Different money.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That's not much of an exaggeration. People rushed to spend their salaries the day they got paid, before the money lost value.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Supermarkets used loudspeakers to announce new prices during the day.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Some shops simply closed, because by the time they restocked, they had lost money on everything they sold.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina needed something drastic. And in 1991, it tried the most drastic idea of all.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The plan was called Convertibility. From 1991, one Argentine peso would be worth exactly one US dollar.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Not roughly. Exactly. And by law, the central bank could only print a peso if it had a real dollar in the vault to back it.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In other words, Argentina took the printing press away from itself.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And it worked. Almost overnight, inflation collapsed. Within a few years, prices were barely rising at all.

visual.caption: President Carlos Menem (right) at the White House

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Foreign money poured back in.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Around the same time, the government sold off state companies, from the phone network to the national airline.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentines who had lived through 1989 could finally save in their own banks again.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But a currency tied to the dollar has a catch.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: When the dollar got strong in the late 1990s, the peso got strong with it, whether that suited Argentina or not.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Its exports became expensive.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Then in 1999, its biggest neighbour and trading partner, Brazil, cut the value of its own currency.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Suddenly, Brazilian goods were cheap and Argentine goods were not.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina slipped into recession.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: To keep paying its bills and defend the one-to-one promise, the government borrowed more and more in dollars.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And investors began to wonder whether the promise could last.

segments.speaker: CUSTOMER
segments.text: Hello! I'd like to take out my savings, please.

segments.speaker: BANK_TELLER
segments.text: Of course. You can have two hundred and fifty pesos.

segments.speaker: CUSTOMER
segments.text: I have twenty thousand in here.

segments.speaker: BANK_TELLER
segments.text: Yes. Two hundred and fifty. This week.

segments.speaker: CUSTOMER
segments.text: And next week?

segments.speaker: BANK_TELLER
segments.text: Two hundred and fifty. Probably.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That was real. In December 2001, with people rushing to pull their money out,

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: the government froze bank accounts and limited withdrawals to 250 pesos a week.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentines called it the corralito, the little fence. It made people furious.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Protesters filled the streets banging pots and pans.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The president resigned and left the palace by helicopter.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In under two weeks, Argentina went through five presidents.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And the country stopped paying its debts: around 132 billion dollars, at the time the largest government default in history.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The peso was cut loose from the dollar and lost most of its value.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Savings people thought were safe in dollars were turned back into pesos worth a fraction as much.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Unemployment passed twenty percent. By late 2002, more than half of all Argentines were living below the poverty line.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: If this story is giving you something to think about, hit subscribe. No fences, no withdrawal limits.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And then, just like in 1870, the grass came to the rescue. Or rather, the soybeans.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In the 2000s, China's booming cities needed food, and the price of soybeans soared.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina's farms were perfectly placed to grow them.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Money flowed back in, the economy grew fast, and for a few years it looked like the comeback story of the century.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But the old habits came back too. Governments spent heavily when times were good.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: When the commodity boom faded, they turned once again to printing money. Inflation crept back, then galloped.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 2014, a long legal fight with foreign creditors pushed Argentina into default again.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 2020, it defaulted for the ninth time in its history.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the end of 2023, prices were rising at more than two hundred percent a year.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And ordinary Argentines did what generations before them had learned to do.

segments.speaker: GRANDSON
segments.text: Grandma, why don't you put your savings in the bank?

segments.speaker: GRANDMOTHER
segments.text: I did. In 1989. And in 2001.

segments.speaker: GRANDSON
segments.text: So where is your money now?

segments.speaker: GRANDMOTHER
segments.text: Somewhere safe.

segments.speaker: GRANDSON
segments.text: In pesos?

segments.speaker: GRANDMOTHER
segments.text: Don't be ridiculous. In dollars.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Economists estimate Argentines hold a huge amount of their savings in US dollars outside the banking system,

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: in safety boxes, in drawers and under mattresses.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: When a country's own people won't hold its money, that tells you everything about trust.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In late 2023, Argentines elected Javier Milei, an economist who campaigned with a chainsaw as a symbol of cutting government spending.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: His government slashed spending and stopped financing the budget by printing money.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Inflation fell sharply: from about 118 percent in 2024 to about 31.5 percent in 2025, the lowest in years,

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: though it was still running at around a third a year by mid-2026.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Supporters say this is the first serious attempt in decades to break the cycle.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Critics point to the pain of the cuts, on wages, pensions and public services, and argue the gains could still unravel.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Economists will be arguing about it for years.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Which brings us back to our question. Why did a country that was once richer than France keep falling?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Let's put the whole story together.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: A sea of grass. British railways all pointing to one port. Frozen beef sailing to London.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Millions of immigrants and a city that called itself the Paris of South America.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: A crash in New York, a coup in Buenos Aires. Factories, wages, and a printing press.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Prices that changed between breakfast and dinner. One peso for one dollar.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: A little fence around everyone's savings. And a grandmother's mattress full of dollars.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So what actually happened to Argentina? There's no single villain. Most economists point to three problems that fed on each other.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: First, the country got rich selling a few crops to a few buyers.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That made it wealthy when prices were high, and fragile when they fell.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It never fully built the wide base of industries and skills that keeps richer countries steady through bad years.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Second, the rules never stayed the same for long.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Coups, counter-coups and governments that undid each other's work meant no plan lasted long enough to pay off.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Investors, farmers and families learned not to plan more than a few years ahead.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And third, again and again, governments paid their bills by printing money.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Every time, prices rose, savings melted, and trust broke a little more.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Once people stop trusting a country's money, it is incredibly hard to win them back. Argentina has spent more than half a century trying.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The lesson isn't really about Argentina.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Natural wealth can make a country rich for a while. What keeps it rich are boring things:

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: stable rules, money people trust, and an economy that doesn't depend on one lucky product.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina still has the Pampas. It still has the soil, the farms and some of the most educated people in Latin America.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Whether it can finally hold on to its wealth this time is a question nobody can answer yet.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: If you made it all the way here, thank you. Subscribe to Farthing Explains for more stories about how money makes and breaks countries.
segments.ctaText: Thanks for watching. Subscribe to Farthing Explains.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Next time, we'll look at a country with almost no natural resources at all that somehow became one of the richest on Earth. See you there.
